clue.text: Gold ring in lounge with paper maybe not far from …

indicators.note: the ring and the gold are placed in the middle of the word for lounging

parts.note: to lounge is to loll
a ring is round, like the letter O
OR is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Someone lounging in gold jewellery with a newspaper, apparently near something else.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into 5 across: this paper sits not far from the bath mat. 'in' puts O and OR inside LOLL.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilet tissue is a kind of paper, and it hangs in the bathroom close to the mat.

clue.text: Nothing and none 18 between those at 26 24

definitions.meaning: with 18 across, 'no ... lost' describes the feeling between enemies

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads 'no ___ lost' between people at daggers drawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis score of nil is called this, and it is the affection absent between enemies.

clue.text: Unlike those at 26 24, opens letters — a monarch calls

indicators.note: the letters of the word opens are taken and rearranged

parts.note: a king is a monarch
terms are names, what things are called

explanation.surface: A ruler opens his correspondence and makes phone calls, unlike people at war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters' rearranges OPENS into ONSPE.
explanation.definitionFit: People still talking to each other are friendly, not openly hostile.

clue.text: Hobson gave one no work and nothing in cash

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: the zero goes into the slang word for money

parts.note: tin is old slang for money
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Hobson offered someone no job and nothing in money.
explanation.walkthrough: Hobson's choice, from a Cambridge stable owner, means take what is offered or nothing: no real choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobson's choice famously allowed no alternative, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: New is old at work

parts.note: New and Old are both prefixes for the British party, and the word also means work

explanation.walkthrough: New Labour and Old Labour are the two wings of the British party; labour also simply means work.
explanation.definitionFit: The party's name precedes both New and Old, and as a verb it means to toil.

clue.text: … spa lacking lustre put under drier?

parts.note: Bath is the English spa town; a bath is also a spa
matt or mat means lacking lustre, not glossy

explanation.surface: A spa resort without sparkle, placed beneath a hairdryer.
explanation.walkthrough: Continuing the 1 across ellipsis. 'drier' is not a machine but a person drying off after bathing, who stands on the mat.
explanation.definitionFit: A small rug is laid beneath someone towelling themselves after a soak.

clue.text: It turned into flowers, having no time to shop

indicators.note: into places the turned word inside the flowers
having no means the abbreviation for time is removed

parts.note: a bouquet is a bunch of flowers

indicators.note: turned means the two letters are read backwards

explanation.surface: Something turned into blooms and then had no time to go shopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' gives TI from IT; 'having no' removes T from BOUQUET, leaving BOUQUE; 'into' puts TI inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fashionable shop is a boutique, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Sitting astride horse, say, with lots of people about

indicators.note: sitting astride means straddling, so the word for sitting surrounds the letter

parts.note: throned means seated on a throne
gee or gee-gee is a word for a horse, written G

explanation.surface: Mounted on a horse among a crowd of onlookers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astride' puts THRONED around G.
explanation.definitionFit: A place filled with a crowd has been crowded or packed with people.

clue.text: One called to defend Hamlet from seeing car, it may be

indicators.note: may be suggests the letters could form something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone summoned to protect Hamlet after he sees a vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet, seeing his father's ghost, cries 'Angels and ministers of grace defend us!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet calls on angelic beings of this kind to protect him from the ghost.

clue.text: Surveyor's report of the more unusual illumination

definitions.note: the possessive means the surveyor's instrument, a noun

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so we listen for how the phrase is spoken

parts.note: the more unusual illumination is the odder light

explanation.surface: A surveyor's account of some very strange lighting.
explanation.definitionFit: A surveying instrument for measuring angles belongs to the surveyor.

clue.text: Call number — does it exist?

parts.note: V is five in Roman numerals
'is it?' asks whether something exists

explanation.surface: A phone call to a number that may not be real.
explanation.definitionFit: To call on someone is to pay them a visit, a synonym.

clue.text: Way of taking insulin — not in beer — for the more mature lady

indicators.note: a way of taking something means it is handled differently, so the letters are rearranged
not tells us to take the word in out of insulin

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice on how a diabetic should take medication without mixing it into beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes IN from INSULIN, leaving SULIN; 'Way of taking' rearranges SULIN with BEER.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluish hair tint is associated with older women, so the phrase stands for such a lady by metonymy.

clue.text: Top answer changed about — changed radically

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the word for changed surrounds the other piece

parts.note: revised means changed

indicators.note: topping a word removes its first letter

parts.note: a solution is an answer

explanation.surface: A leading answer has been altered, and altered drastically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' takes the S off SOLUTION, leaving OLUTION, and 'about' puts REVISED around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To transform something completely is to bring about a revolution in it.

clue.text: Suffering from as much vertigo as possible is commonly too much

definitions.text: Suffering from as much vertigo as possible

definitions.meaning: a colloquial phrase for something outrageous

explanation.walkthrough: 'That's the giddy limit' is old-fashioned British slang for something beyond what can be tolerated.
explanation.definitionFit: Dizzy to the maximum, and an informal phrase for something outrageously excessive.

clue.text: Black rhyme for Greene's coloured boy

definitions.meaning: Pinky is the boy in Graham Greene's Brighton Rock, and his name is a colour; the answer rhymes with it

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition only describes the word by sound: it rhymes with Pinky, from Greene's novel Brighton Rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stained with ink is very dark, so it means black.

clue.text: Merrymaking before other things that are sad and dreary

parts.note: fun is merrymaking
ere is an old word for before
et al is short for et alia, and other things

explanation.surface: Partying first, then some other gloomy matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mournful and gloomy, like a burial ceremony.

clue.text: Boss me about — stratagem? I'm not sure

indicators.note: about means the little word me is turned round

parts.note: a ploy is a stratagem
er is the hesitant noise of someone unsure

explanation.surface: A worker suspects the manager of scheming against them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who hires and directs staff is their boss.

clue.text: Transmit over cliff to get meat for stew

indicators.note: over means the word for transmit spans across the cliff

parts.note: to send is to transmit
a crag is a steep rock face

explanation.surface: Sending something over a cliff edge to get stewing meat.
explanation.walkthrough: SCRAG END is the bony neck of mutton, a cheap British stewing cut.
explanation.definitionFit: The scrawny neck end of mutton is used for slow-cooked stews.

clue.text: Science involving force with CID's many changes

indicators.note: changes tells us the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Detectives in the CID undergo many reorganisations.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's plain-clothes detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: The branch of mechanics dealing with forces and motion has this name.

clue.text: Missing conclusion to 1 down's 4s

definitions.meaning: the last word of Shakespeare's comedy title formed from 1 down and 4 down plurals

explanation.walkthrough: 1 down and 4 down give Love's Labour's, completed by this word as the title of a Shakespeare play.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mislaid or gone astray is missing.

clue.text: A theologian was in front? That's bad

parts.note: DD is Doctor of Divinity, a theologian
led means was in front

explanation.surface: A divinity scholar took the lead, which is regarded as a bad thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoilt eggs are called rotten, so addled means gone bad.

clue.text: Poodle (but it isn't) turning up as heavenly friend?

indicators.note: turning up in a down clue means the phrase reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a friend in heaven might be a god pal

explanation.surface: A poodle that is not actually a dog, flipped upward as a divine companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poodle' here is the political sense, a servile follower, and the bracket warns it is not the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A fawning hanger-on is called a poodle or a lapdog, synonyms in politics.

clue.text: Contrasting duo tilt wrong way — tilt has Gerald in trouble

indicators.note: turned the wrong way means these four letters are rearranged

parts.note: to tilt is to lean

indicators.note: being in trouble means the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Two opposites tip over badly, and the tipping leaves Gerald in difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong way' gives LITT from TILT; 'in trouble' turns LEAN plus GERALD into LEANDLARGE. Little and Large were a British TV comedy double act.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedy pair were named for their contrasting physiques, a thin man and a stout one.

clue.text: America's responsibility?

parts.note: split as two words, the reading means it's down to the USA

explanation.walkthrough: Split into ON US, the word means America's to deal with.
explanation.definitionFit: A burden or duty borne by someone; split, it reads as the USA's charge.

clue.text: Big trouble when played for fun underground?

parts.note: merry means full of fun
hell is traditionally imagined beneath the earth

explanation.surface: Serious mischief made by a team playing just for enjoyment below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'play' this is to cause havoc, hence 'when played'; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'play merry hell' means to cause a great disturbance.

clue.text: See 26
Stunned and a bit withered inside

indicators.note: inside places the dried-up word within the small amount

parts.note: a tad is a little bit
sere means dried up and withered

explanation.surface: Dazed and somewhat shrivelled within.
explanation.definitionFit: Being hit with an electric stun gun leaves a person incapacitated.

clue.text: Extreme variance — ††† (pictured)

parts.note: the printed symbols are typographic daggers
drawn means pictured

explanation.surface: A row of dagger symbols illustrating bitter disagreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The symbols are daggers, and they are drawn on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: People at open hostility are said to be at daggers drawn.
